Subject: Recap + next steps: Autoscale SLO qualification

Hi Alex, Samir —

Thanks again for the call today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we keep momentum on the SLO/autoscale conversation:  

Summary of requirements you voiced:
- Target p95 latency: 120ms for synchronous text-generation endpoints
- Sustained throughput: 1800 requests/minute during peak windows (mornings ET)
- Concurrency per model: up to 250 concurrent requests (streaming supported)
- Streaming requirement: client-side incremental tokens with max latency between token chunks < 30ms
- Burst tolerance: handle 3x baseline traffic for up to 5 minutes while maintaining p95 < 300ms

Key constraints:
- FastPay prefers a warm-pool model (keep N hot workers per model) to minimize cold-start tail latency
- Ops needs predictable scale-up times (target < 90s to reach full burst capacity)

Attachments: I’ve attached a filled SLO worksheet and a short sketch of our autoscale design for reference.

Proposed next steps:
1) Neha & Vivek to confirm technical feasibility and provide recommended warm-pool sizing + estimated scale-up times (ETA: 48 hours)  
2) FastPay to share recent traffic slice (1 week sample with 1-min resolution) and any historical bursts so we can run a sizing simulation  
3) Schedule a short POC prep call to align on metrics we’ll measure (can do Wed or Thu next week)

Can you confirm the traffic sample and whether the 3x/5min burst target is the correct policy to qualify for burst capacity? Once we have that, we’ll run a quick simulator and come back with recommendations.

Thanks —
Marissa
Director, Strategic Accounts
Redwood Inference

Thanks Marissa — good summary. Quick clarifications from our side:  

- p95 120ms is the aspirational target; we can accept p95 up to 150ms for short bursts but want <120ms for sustained traffic.
- Sustained throughput: 1800 req/min is correct for our current peak (we expect 10% growth/quarter).
- Concurrency: 250 concurrent streaming requests is conservative; we've seen short spikes up to ~400 concurrent during promo events. We absolutely need graceful degradation beyond 250 (queueing or degraded rate), not hard failures.
- Burst: 3x for 5 minutes is our baseline ask. For marketing promos we sometimes see 5x for 2 minutes.

We’ll share the 1-week traffic sample (anonymized) by EOD tomorrow. Also looping in our ops alias (ops@fastpay.com) — they’ll share historical burst windows and any SLO docs.

Appreciate the warm-pool approach — if you can propose warm-pool counts and warm-up times, that will help our capacity planning.

—Alex
VP Product, FastPay

Hi Alex/Samir —

Great context — a couple of quick technical questions to size warm pools and scale-up:  

1) Model variants: are you planning to serve a single production model (v1.3) across all traffic, or will you have multiple variants (v1.2/v1.3 Canary)? Warm pools are per-model-variant and we need to account for split traffic.
2) Average request token length and generation budget: what’s the median prompt size and median completion length? This affects GPU memory and throughput per worker.
3) Acceptable queueing behavior: do you prefer request queuing with a soft-degrade (longer latency) or immediate 429s when beyond concurrency? For SLOs we typically recommend queueing with an adaptive timeout and prioritized traffic lanes.
4) Warm pool budget: if we provision N warm workers, what percentage of peak traffic do you want to cover from the warm pool (eg. 50% of 3x burst)?

Initial internal estimate (very rough): to hit p95 <150ms for 250 concurrent streaming requests with typical 50-token generation, we’d start with a warm pool of ~40 workers for the model variant, and expect scale-up to 3x baseline in ~70-110s depending on cloud autoscale latency and image pull times. We can refine once we get token metrics and traffic slices.

If you can send the traffic sample and token-size stats, I’ll run the simulator and share a recommended warm-pool sizing matrix by EOD Thursday.

Thanks —
Neha
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
